```{r setup, echo=FALSE, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE)
```

`mpathsenser` 2.0.0 is a breaking release. Databases cannot be upgraded in
place, several functions are gone, and some columns have changed. This guide
describes the changes that most often require edits to a script written for
1.2.4. The [NEWS](../news/index.html) lists every change, and
the [Get started article](mpathsenser.html) shows the new workflow from start
to finish.

In short:

- Create a new database with `create_db()` and import the JSON files again with
  `read_mpath_sense()`; old databases are not migrated.
- Replace calls to `import()`, `coverage()`, and the other functions listed
  below.
- Check scripts that use the `date` or `measurement_id` columns, the
  `AppUsage` `start`/`end` columns, or the sensors that are no longer imported.

## Create a new database and import again

Version 2.0.0 uses DuckDB instead of SQLite. An existing 1.2.4 database cannot
be opened or converted, so create a new database and import the original
m-Path Sense files into it. The JSON files are the source of truth, so
re-importing is the intended way to upgrade.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
path <- "path/to/m-path-sense-json"
db <- create_db("path/to/study-2.0.duckdb")
read_mpath_sense(path = path, db = db)
```

`create_db()` and `open_db()` accept either a full file path or a directory
and a file name, and they open the database read-only when you ask them to:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
create_db("path/to/study-2.0.duckdb")
create_db("path/to", "study-2.0.duckdb")
create_db(path = NULL)                    # in-memory database
open_db("path/to/study-2.0.duckdb", read_only = TRUE)
```

The old default database name (`sense.db`) is gone, so `create_db()` no longer
creates a database from a directory alone, and `open_db()` requires a path.
Both functions also accept `threads`, `memory_limit`, and `temp_directory` to
control how DuckDB uses the machine.

`read_mpath_sense()` is the replacement for `import()` and keeps the familiar
`path`, `sensors`, and `recursive` arguments. The `backend` argument is gone
because DuckDB is the only backend, and the default `batch_size` is now 1000.
Two new arguments control what happens after importing: `deduplicate` and
`optimize` both default to `TRUE`. There is no parallel import; DuckDB
parallelises internally, and a database accepts only one writer at a time.

Every 2.0.0 database records its own layout version. `open_db()` refuses a
database whose version it does not know and points you to `create_db()`.
Databases from development versions that predate versioning are opened with a
warning. If you just want to look around, `example_db()` opens a small example
database that ships with the package.

If you wrote SQL against the old table names, note that sensor data now lives
in internal tables, with read-only per-sensor views in front of them. Package
functions such as `get_data()` read from those views, and you normally should
too.

## Removed functions and objects

| Removed in 2.0.0 | Replacement |
| --- | --- |
| `import()` | `read_mpath_sense()` |
| `coverage()` | `coverage_frequency()` and `coverage_proportional()`; see [Coverage](#coverage) |
| `freq` | `coverage_expected()` supplies the default expected intervals |
| `ccopy()` | `base::file.copy()` |
| `fix_jsons()`, `test_jsons()` | `jsonlite::validate()`; `unzip_data()` or `utils::unzip()` for zip files |
| `first_date()`, `last_date()` | Read the first and last `time` with `get_data()`; see the example below |
| `with_localtime()` | `to_local_time()`, `collect_local()`, or the `_local` views; see [Times and timezones](#times-and-timezones) |
| `link_db()` | `link()` |
| `index_db()` | Nothing: DuckDB keeps its own statistics, so manual indexes are not needed |
| `vacuum_db()` | Nothing: DuckDB manages the database file; use `optimize_db()` to keep tables in good shape |
| `decrypt_gps()` | Decrypt before importing: the new importer reads coordinates as numbers only |

`first_date()` and `last_date()` used to return the first and last date of one
sensor. Use `get_data()` with `summarise()` instead:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
get_data(db, sensor = "Accelerometer", participant_id = "12345") |>
  summarise(
    first = min(time, na.rm = TRUE),
    last = max(time, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  collect()
```

Two arguments that used to accept `"All"` for every sensor now want `NULL`:

| 1.2.4 | 2.0.0 |
| --- | --- |
| `copy_db(db1, db2, sensor = "All")` | `copy_db(db1, db2, sensor = NULL)` |
| `get_nrows(db, sensor = "All")` | `get_nrows(db, sensor = NULL)` |

A few other arguments changed name or are no longer available:

| 1.2.4 | 2.0.0 |
| --- | --- |
| `import(path, db, backend = "RSQLite")` | `read_mpath_sense(path, db)` |
| `create_db(path = tempdir())` | `create_db("study.duckdb")` or `create_db(tempdir(), "study.duckdb")` |
| `open_db()` | `open_db(path)`: the path is required |
| `unzip_data()` | `unzip_data(path)`: the path is required |
| `moving_average(..., n = 60)` | `moving_average(..., window = 60)`; see [`moving_average()`](#moving_average) |
| `link(..., split = "participant_id")` | Omit `split`; it is deprecated and ignored |

`copy_db()` also requires the target database to be a file, not an in-memory
database.

## Times and timezones

Timestamps are stored as the moment an observation happened, not as a clock
reading. When you collect data with `get_data()`, `time` is a `POSIXct` vector
in UTC. Version 1.2.4 returned timestamps as text, so code that compared them
as strings needs to switch to date-time comparisons.

If the imported files contain `Timezone` measurements, the import assigns each
measurement the timezone that applied when the measurement started. The result
is stored in the `timezone` column. In 1.2.4 this was a separate step; now it
happens during import. If some measurements have no timezone yet,
`add_timezones_to_db()` fills in the missing values from the `Timezone` data.
It never overwrites a timezone that is already set, so running it again is
safe.

To show times the way a participant experienced them, read a `_local` view, or
convert the data yourself:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
# Both local time and the absolute time
get_data(db, sensor = "Activity_with_local")

# Local time replaces the timestamp
get_data(db, sensor = "Activity_local")

# Convert after collecting
get_data(db, sensor = "Activity", participant_id = "12345") |>
  collect_local()

# Or convert one column
get_data(db, sensor = "Activity", participant_id = "12345") |>
  mutate(time = to_local_time(time, timezone)) |>
  collect()
```

Keep the `timezone` column next to any converted timestamp; a local clock time
alone does not say which moment it refers to. If no timezone is known, local
time falls back to UTC. `to_local_time()` accepts one timezone for all rows or
one per row.

Local clock times can be ambiguous during a daylight-saving change. Use the
UTC view when you sort events or measure elapsed time, and the local view when
you group by the participant's day.

Date filters in `get_data()` are strict. A character value must use
`YYYY-MM-DD`, and a `Date` selects that whole day; a `POSIXt` value selects an
exact moment. Day bounds follow UTC for `time` columns, including the
`_with_local` views, and participant-local time for `_local` views. A
malformed date is now an error instead of a filter that quietly matches
nothing.

Finally, m-Path Sense versions 6 and older recorded some timestamps as local
clock values. The new importer recognises those fields and preserves their
clock time, so re-importing old files gives better times than before.

## Coverage

`coverage()` has been split into two functions with clearer meanings:

- `coverage_frequency()` counts how many measurements were recorded.
- `coverage_proportional()` compares the data with what was expected, either
  as a count, as covered time, or as filled time slots.

Both use expected sampling intervals that you provide as named values.
`coverage_expected()` supplies the package defaults and replaces the old `freq`
vector:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
coverage_frequency(db, sensor = "Accelerometer", by = "hour")

coverage_proportional(
  db,
  expected = coverage_expected(),
  sensor = "Accelerometer",
  metric = "count",
  by = "hour"
)
```

The calculation runs in the database and the result stays lazy until you
`collect()` it. `plot()` draws the result as a line chart or a heatmap. For the
sensors that iOS does not provide (`AppUsage`, `Light`, `Memory`, and
`Screen`), coverage for iOS participants is `NA`.

## `moving_average()`

`moving_average()` is still experimental, but the `n` argument (a number of
rows) has been replaced by `window` (an amount of time). A number is still
seconds, so `n = 60` becomes `window = 60`, or write `window = "1 minute"`:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
# 1.2.4
moving_average(db, sensor = "Accelerometer", cols = "x_mean", n = 60)

# 2.0.0
moving_average(db, sensor = "Accelerometer", cols = "x_mean", window = 60)
```

The window is centered on each measurement and spans the given amount of time,
not a number of rows: with `window = 60`, a measurement at 12:00:00 averages
everything from 11:59:30 through 12:00:30, including both ends. Each
measurement in the window counts once, so a busy period has more influence
than a quiet one. Participant and date filters are applied first, and the
result stays in the database until you collect it. Windows expressed in months
or years are not allowed, because their length depends on the calendar.

## Files, duplicates, and re-importing

A file is recognised by its name, size, and modification time. Unchanged files
are skipped on a later import, so re-importing a folder after a few new files
have arrived is cheap. A renamed copy of an old file is imported again.

Duplicates are removed after importing. A measurement is identified by
`participant_id` and `time`, plus extra fields where a sensor can record
several measurements at the same moment (for example, the app in `AppUsage`).
When a measurement occurs more than once, the copy from the newest file wins;
within that file, the last row as written wins. This keeps completed interval
windows and Garmin's recalculated values. Measurements that occur only once
are never touched, so a corrected re-upload does not remove data that was
missing from the correction.

Files are imported oldest to newest, which is what makes the newest file win.
`deduplicate_db()` performs the same cleanup across the whole database; run it
if an import was interrupted.

`get_processed_files()` shows the file ledger: one row per imported file with
its `file_id`, size, modification time, sense version, and processing time.
The old `study_id` column is gone; join through `Participant` if you need the
study.

## Sensors and columns that changed

Ten sensors are no longer imported because m-Path Sense no longer records
them: `AirQuality`, `Calendar`, `Geofence`, `Gyroscope`, `InstalledApps`,
`Keyboard`, `Mobility`, `Noise`, `PhoneLog`, and `TextMessage`. Re-imported
data will not contain them. Installed apps are still available:
`installed_apps()` now derives them from `AppUsage`.

Some columns changed as well:

- `measurement_id` and `date` are gone from every sensor table. Use
  `participant_id` and `time` (plus sensor-specific fields) to identify a
  measurement. To select a day, use the `start_date` and `end_date` arguments
  of `get_data()`, or derive a day with `as.Date(time)` after collecting.
- `AppUsage` renamed `start` and `end` to `period_start` and `period_end`.
- `Bluetooth` no longer has `bluetooth_device_type`.
- `Device` no longer has `sdk`, and `device_info()` no longer returns the raw
  device payload.
- Garmin `zeroCrossing` data uses `deadband` (all lowercase), not the old
  misspelled `deadBand`.
- Participant ids are stored as numbers, so `get_participants()` returns a
  numeric `participant_id` instead of text. Filtering with a character value
  still works.
- `sensors` is now in alphabetical order. Since the CRAN 1.2.4 release it has
  also gained `BluetoothBeacon` and the Garmin sensors.

## Concurrent access and housekeeping

A DuckDB database allows one writer at a time. Keep a single import or
maintenance process per database, and open extra connections with
`read_only = TRUE` for dashboards or other readers. If another process has the
database open for writing, `open_db()` says so instead of failing silently.

`optimize_db()` re-orders the sensor tables so that filters on participant and
time can skip data more efficiently. The import already does this for the
sensors it touches; run it by hand after a large import if you disabled that.

## What stays the same

The everyday workflow is unchanged: create a database, import files, query
with `get_data()`, then use dplyr verbs before collecting. `get_data()` still
returns a lazy table, `sensors` still lists the supported sensors, and
functions such as `link()`, `link_gaps()`, `identify_gaps()`, `add_gaps()`,
`bin_data()`, `haversine()`, `geocode_rev()`, `app_category()`,
`get_participants()`, `get_studies()`, `get_nrows()`, `get_processed_files()`,
`installed_apps()`, and `device_info()` remain available, with the argument
changes noted above.
